questions.question: Why are strings immutable in Go?
questions.title: String Immutability
questions.direct_answer: Remember: strings are read-only byte views — s[0] = 'H' won't compile. Change requires building a new string. Makes them safe to share, copy, hash (map keys), and pass across goroutines.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand String Immutability beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its complexity or failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Remember: strings are read-only byte views — s[0] = 'H' won't compile. Change requires building a new string. Makes them safe to share, copy, hash (map keys), and pass across.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
A Go string is a read-only view over bytes, and the language enforces it: s[0] = 'H' fails to compile. What you CAN do: read bytes (s[0] is a byte value), slice substrings (both share memory — no copy), build NEW strings.

```go
s := "hello"
// s[0] = 'H'    // compile error
b := []byte(s)
b[0] = 'H'
fmt.Println(string(b), s)   // Hello hello — original untouched
```

Executed. Converting to []byte, mutating the copy, converting back — the original is untouched, because string(b) allocates a new string.

Why the language chose immutability: a string value is two words — pointer + length, no capacity, no writes. If strings were mutable, every assignment would either copy bytes (expensive) or share writable memory (one write corrupts another's view). Immutable bytes make the two-word header completely safe to copy — assignment is copying pointer+len, which is why strings are so cheap to pass.

The consequences: comparable with ==, hashable (map keys — bytes can't change so the hash can't rot), safe across goroutines (read-only can't race), O(1) slicing (shares memory).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[str: ptr to read-only bytes, len] --> IMM[no writes through s]
    B[[]byte copy] --> MUT[mutable - capacity field]
    SL[s 1:3] --> SH[shares s bytes - O1]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The runtime representation: a string is (data-pointer, length) — two machine words, no capacity field, never written through the string type. Every mutating-looking operation — ToUpper, string(b), Replace — allocates a new string; the original's bytes are untouched, because no path exists to write through them.

Why []byte is the mutable counterpart: a []byte has the three-word header (pointer, length, CAPACITY) — the capacity field enables append, and the data is writable. Converting string(b) copies bytes into a fresh immutable allocation; []byte(s) copies into a fresh mutable one. Both directions COPY — the API's honest signal that you crossed a mutability boundary.

The performance folklore: converting string-back-and-forth in a LOOP is the classic Go allocation hotspot. The idioms: strings.Builder for building (mutable buffer, one String() at the end), strings.Map for transforms (returns the ORIGINAL when nothing changed — the runtime checks), bytes.Buffer when the data was always bytes.

The substring-sharing subtlety: s[1:3] shares s's underlying bytes — O(1), no copy. A tiny substring of a huge string keeps the WHOLE huge backing alive (the substring's pointer anchors the parent's start). That's why long-running services use strings.Clone (Go 1.18+) when storing small pieces of large parsed inputs — it breaks the anchor.

questions.question: What is the zero value of a string in Go?
questions.title: When would you use String Immutability in a real project
questions.direct_answer: "" (the empty string) — NOT nil. A declared-but-unset string is immediately usable: len 0, concatenation works, comparisons work. No nil state exists for the string type.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: "" (the empty string) — NOT nil.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The zero value is "" — an empty string, fully usable:

```go
var s string          // ""
len(s)                  // 0
s + "more"               // "more"
s == ""                  // true
fmt.Sprintf("<%s>", s) // "<>"
```

There is no nil string. This differs from the other header types: slice zero is nil, map zero is nil, pointer zero is nil — but string's zero is a valid empty string.

The mechanics: a nil-able type is a POINTER to a structure that can be absent. A string is (pointer, length) where pointer-nil + length-0 IS the empty string — the representation of "" is exactly (nil, 0), a coherent value.

Practical consequence: strings never need nil-check ceremony. Emptiness is s == "" or len(s) == 0.

The JSON boundary case: an empty string marshals to \"\" never null; to express 'absent', *string (pointer to string) is the type — its nil marshals as null. When an API needs to distinguish 'absent' from 'empty', that's the tool.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    N[nil ptr + 0 len] --> E[empty string]
    E --> OK[fully valid - no nil state]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why no nil — the mechanics: a nil-able type is a POINTER to a structure that can be absent. A map's nil has no hash table; a slice's nil has no backing array. A string is (pointer, length) where pointer-nil plus length-zeronil, 0), a coherent value  rather than an absence.

The design consequence vs other header types: slices and maps need nil-check ceremony (a nil map write panics; a nil slice can't be indexed) — strings need none. Every operation works on "": len, comparison, slicing (""[0:0]), range (zero iterations).

The empty-vs-nil boundary cases: (1) JSON — a string marshals as \"\" never null; to express 'absent' in JSON, *string is the type — APIs that need the distinction document it; (2) SQL nullable columns — database drivers use sql.NullString (a struct {String string; Valid bool}) — the standard library's own admission that the string type can't express null and the workaround is a wrapper. Knowing NullString exists signals production experience with nullable text columns.

The deeper consequence: the zero-value design means every API taking a string never needs the nil ceremony — a signature (s string) is complete as written.

questions.question: Why does concatenating strings in a loop perform badly, and what should you use instead?
questions.title: a common mistake when using String Immutability
questions.direct_answer: Each + allocates a new string and copies everything before it — N concatenations cost O(N²) copies. Use strings.Builder: one growing buffer, one final copy. Or strings.Join for the separator case.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Each + allocates a new string and copies everything before it — N concatenations cost O(N²) copies. Use strings.Builder: one growing buffer, one final copy. Or strings.Join for the separator.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    L[+= loop] --> C[copy 1c, 2c, 3c...]
    C --> Q[On2 total]
    BD[Builder] --> G[grow buffer + one final copy]
    G --> OK[On total]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The allocation arithmetic: appending k chunks of size c. First += copies c bytes. Second copies 2c. Third 3c. Total: c·k(k+1)/2 — O(k²) bytes copied for O(k·c) work.

Builder's mechanics: internally a []byte with append growth. WriteString appends (amortized O(1) per write); String() does ONE final copy. Grow(n) pre-allocates when the final size is knowable.

Why the compiler can't fix += automatically: Go's string is immutable, so s += x MUST produce a new string. The compiler folds some adjacent patterns, but the general loop case can't know the final size ahead — the quadratic cost is semantic, not an implementation accident. That's why the fix is an API (Builder) rather than a compiler pass.

The measurement: benchmarking += 10,000 times vs Builder — the += version is typically 100-1000x slower at that scale, entirely allocation. The Go 1.10 Builder release notes cite exactly this pattern.

questions.question: What happens when you slice a string in Go — does it copy?
questions.title: compare String Immutability with an alternative
questions.direct_answer: s[1:3] does NOT copy — the substring shares the original's underlying bytes (O(1), just a new pointer+len). Both strings stay alive together; use strings.Clone to break the anchor.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: s[1:3] does NOT copy — the substring shares the original's underlying bytes (O(1), just a new pointer+len).

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Slicing a string is O(1) and shares memory — the substring is a new (pointer, length) header pointing INTO the original's bytes:

```go
s := "hello world"
sub := s[0:5]     // "hello" — no copy, shares s's bytes
```

The sharing is invisible to correct code (strings are immutable — neither can change the bytes), but it has a lifetime consequence: the substring's pointer anchors the original's memory. A tiny 5-byte substring of a 10MB parsed document keeps all 10MB alive as long as the substring exists.

That's the bug shape in long-running services: parse a huge payload, save a small token from it, drop the payload — but the token silently holds the whole thing. The fix is strings.Clone (Go 1.18+), which copies just the substring's bytes into a fresh allocation:

```go
token := strings.Clone(s[start:end])   // fresh small string, original collectable
```

The related facts: slicing works on BYTES (can slice mid-rune — producing invalid UTF-8 if you're not careful with boundaries); the slice bounds are byte indices; and the same sharing applies to []byte slices (the append-gotcha family from the slices topic — but for strings, no append exists to fork them apart).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    S[10MB string] --> SL[s 0:5 - new 5-byte header]
    SL -->|ptr aims into| S
    CL[strings.Clone] --> NEW[fresh 5-byte copy]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The memory layout, concretely: s := "hello world" compiles to (ptr→[104 101 108 108 111 32 119 ...], len 11). sub := s[0:5] compiles to (ptr→SAME bytes, len 5) — one pointer addition at slice time (ptr advances by the start index), zero bytes moved. That's the entire O(1).

The GC consequence — the mechanism of the anchor: Go's garbage collector traces reachability. While sub is reachable, its pointer makes the 11-byte allocation reachable — the whole allocation, because sub's pointer aims into its interior. The GC has no concept of 'only the first 5 bytes matter' — liveness is per-allocation. So the 10MB-payload case is literal: one small live string pins one large dead-except-for-it allocation.

Why strings.Clone was added (Go 1.18): the anchor pattern was a known memory-leak class in servers — strings.Fields/config parsers/logging pipelines all produce small strings carved from large inputs. Before Clone, the fixes were manual copies (string([]byte(sub)) — an idiom nobody understood was a memory fix); Clone names the intent and is the canonical answer. For []byte, append([]byte(nil), sub...) is the equivalent.

The correctness boundary alongside the lifetime one: s[a:b] slices bytes, so rune-aware code needs offsets from range iteration (the strings topic's core) — a substring cut mid-rune yields invalid UTF-8 that later decodes to U+FFFD. Two independent reasons to be deliberate with string slicing: memory (anchor) and encoding (rune boundaries).

questions.question: How do you safely modify string contents in Go?
questions.title: debug a problem involving String Immutability
questions.direct_answer: Convert to a mutable type ([]byte or []rune), change, convert back — each conversion copies. Or use strings.Replace/Map which return NEW strings. You never write through a string.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Repeating a definition without saying when to use it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give one trade-off and say how you would test it.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Recall: Convert to a mutable type ([]byte or []rune), change, convert back — each conversion copies.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
There's no in-place edit — the path is always convert → mutate → convert:

```go
s := "hello"
b := []byte(s)      // copy to mutable bytes
b[0] = 'H'
s2 := string(b)      // copy back — "Hello" (s unchanged)

r := []rune(s)       // copy to mutable runes
r[0] = 'H'
s3 := string(r)      // "Hello" — rune-safe for multibyte
```

Executed earlier: the original stays "hello" every time.

The []byte vs []rune choice: byte for ASCII-safe/binary handling (faster, one byte per element); rune when changing CHARACTER content (each element is a code point — a multibyte char replaces as one element, never corrupts).

The functional alternative — when the change is a transform, use the transform functions (which allocate internally and return new strings):

```go
strings.ToUpper(s)
strings.Replace(s, "l", "L", 1)
strings.Map(func(r rune) rune { if r == 'l' { return 'L' }; return r }, s)
```

strings.Map's subtlety: it returns the ORIGINAL string (zero alloc) when the function changes nothing — the runtime checks for identity. That's the closest Go gets to in-place: avoiding the copy when no change happened.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    STR[string] -->|[]byte| BYT[mutable bytes]
    BYT -->|edit| BYT2[changed]
    BYT2 -->|string b| STR2[new string]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why the round-trip is two copies and why that's the honest cost: []byte(s) copies bytes into a mutable buffer (the string can't hand out writable access to read-only memory); string(b) copies into a fresh immutable allocation (the buffer could change again — the conversion must snapshot). Immutability's price is paid at each boundary crossing, and that's WHY the API has no 'modify in place' — no such state exists on the string side.

The rune conversion's extra work: []rune(s) DECODES UTF-8 to code points (O(n) with per-rune decoding work), string(r) RE-ENCODES. The byte round-trip is two memcpys; the rune round-trip is decode + encode. ASCII input makes them nearly identical; heavy multibyte content widens the gap. Choosing []rune is correctness (character-level edits), not speed.

strings.Map's zero-copy fast path, mechanically: it writes output to a buffer lazily — the first changed rune triggers buffer allocation and backfill of prior runes; if the map function returns every input rune unchanged, the original pointer is returned untouched. For 'usually no changes' workloads (validation that occasionally rewrites), that's a free win — and a behavior worth knowing because callers can compare pointer identity (unsafe but real) to detect the no-change case.

The full toolkit by job: one substring change → strings.Replace; systematic transform → strings.Map or ToUpper; many edits → []rune once, edit the slice, string(r) once (not repeated conversions — the batch-then-convert pattern, the same amortization lesson as Builder); binary data → []byte the whole way (it was never text).
